1. What do you notice? I noticed that people in the 18 to 29 were the group most in favor of college athletes being paid. And as each group get's older in age, they are less in favor of college athletes being paid. This is likely due to younger generations siding with student athletes their age, while older age groups are sticking to more traditional ideas. 

2. What do you wonder? I wonder why so many more men think college athletes should be paid than women. If I had to guess, this might be because men are more likely to be invested in money dominant sports like football and basketball. I also wonder how many people on the graph were athletes in high school and college. I think someones athletic background is essential to this topic, as someone with no interest in sports may not be sure. 

3. What impact does this have you and your community? Even though I don't think I will play competitive sports in college, being a high school athlete has shown me how much dedication and hard work it takes to be an athlete. I have friends and family who are or have played college sports at a high level, and that commitment is on a whole other level. With all the hard work college athletes put in, they deserve to be rewarded.

comments.raw_comment:
1. What do you notice? If your notice makes a claim, where in the graph is the evidence to support it?

I notice that people within the 18-29 age range for the most part strongly agree that college athletes should be paid. As you move up you can notice that this view shifts in the opposite direction, as 60% of participants in the 60 or older age range believe that college athletes should not be paid. I also notice that white people, as well as women, and senior citizens also seem to lean towards the idea of college athletes not being paid.

2. What do you wonder?

I wonder if there are different societal pressures and expectations among all these groups of people and how that may affect their opinions on whether or not college athletes should be paid. I also wonder if racial minorities vote higher on paying athletes due to wage discrimination and the upsetting history that our country has when it comes to the topic of race and pay equality.

3. What impact does this have on you and your community?
While I don’t plan on becoming a college athlete, I have many friends and peers who see themselves playing a sport in college. Payment for college athletes could have an impact on the expenses that they may have to pay for potential injuries as well as helping to minimize the amount of college debt that the student will have to pay off post-college. 

4. What's going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the graph's main idea.

“College Athletes: Pay or No Play”

The least number of those voting "no" are in the 60+ age group. They also have the greatest number of "unsure" voters. This is probably because collegiate athletics are not popular among persons in that age group. I also see that more white voters than other ethnic groups and more female voters than male voters declined to participate in the poll.

2) I'm curious as to why more white people declined than Black or Latino people. I would have wanted to see the outcomes for voters from various socioeconomic backgrounds.

3) Because I am at the age where college sports recruiting is most common, I can most directly connect to this. I am familiar with numerous folks my age who have recently made commitments or are now seeking employment.

4) Play or Pay.

comments.raw_comment:
1) What do you notice? I notice that most adults believe that the younger generation of athletes should get paid by colleges. The percentage is significant, 70% of adults think colleges should pay their athletes from ages 18 to 29. The other age groups are either 50/50 or more adults who think colleges shouldn’t pay their athletes.

2) What do you wonder? I wonder why more adults think the athletes that are minorities should get paid by their colleges than white athletes. I wonder if it has to do with the fact that the minorities do not have as many resources as white people do. There are many athletes with potential but are limited which deprives them from becoming professionals.

3) How does this relate to you and your community? This relates to me and my community because I live in an area that is home to mostly hispanics. My hispanic peers and myself are incredibly talented like any other race. Yet money is still a major factor in everything we do. I see many of my peers who would like to do more but face limitations due to their status. When given the opportunity they are able to reach their full potential. An example of this is financial aid for upcoming college students, this paves the way for many people who would like to pursue an education but do not possess the money themselves to fully pay for college.

1. This graph shows the data of what people think about the topic, separated between race, gender, and age. Between yes and no there are still some people that are unsure. Yet it is hard to tell how many people are unsure in total because the figures don't add up to 100. In age: 18-44 more than 50% say yes to athletes who should get paid by their college.  45-60 both have 60% that say no to athletes getting paid. More men are saying yes to athletes getting paid, this could lead into having more male athletes.

3. This relates to the community by benefitting low income communities. When athletes come from a low income community they would be able to benefit from being paid by their college. Their family will also benefit from this. By providing money for them they will be guaranteed good resources, supplies, and health.

comments.raw_comment:
I noticed that young male Black and Latino participants favored colleges paying their athletes more than the other participants did. I believe it's because this demographic tends to depend on college sports to support their educations, so they personally benefit from athletes being paid.

I wonder why so many women answered no to the survey. Although the college sport community  tends to be dominated by men, there are many skilled female athletes that could benefit from being paid for their work so I would've assumed there would have been more women who were for the cause.

This doesn't relate to me personally, seeing as I'm not a serious athlete, nor am I close to anyone who seeks to be one. However, I am aware that within my community, there are many teens who look forward to playing sports in college and they are most likely to be very passionate on this subject.

In the graph, we see the opinions of different demographics on the topic of college athletes being paid, and there are a few simple conclusions that can be drawn from it. One headline that would go well with this graph is "Colleges Profit off of D1 Sports. Should the Athletes Get a Cut?"

For instance, are men more likely to support college-paying athletes because sports are a part of male gender norms? Do certain cultures value sports more than others? The decision of whether to pay or not pay college athletes can affect whether athletes go into sports in college and other financial decisions surrounding sports. I notice that older people generally do not think colleges should pay their athletes. As age increases, votes saying colleges should not pay their athletes increase. What do you wonder?
I am most curious about the disparity in votes between races. I wonder why more whites said no than the Black or Latino groups. I would have liked to see the results for voters across multiple income levels. 
How does this relate to you?
This relates most to me because I am at the age where college recruitment for sports is most prevalent. I know many people my age who have recently committed or are in the recruitment process currently.

comments.raw_comment:
Thanks to all students who participated!

Here are some of the catchy headlines that we received:  "Split Views on Paying College Athletes" by Finn and Olivia of Cookeville, Tennessee; “Should Athletic Commitment Come with Pay?” by Janay of Philadelphia; “Paid to Play?  Or Not Today?” by Danaher of Berkley, Michigan; “College Athlete Compensation: Yes or No?” by Sophia of Andover High School in Massachusetts; "Should College Athletes Be Making Bucks" by Diego, and "Are Scholarships Enough to Pay Our Star Athletes?" by Bryn and Edwin of Eaglecrest High School in Aurora, Colorado.

You can continue to post comments and replies.  Please check back on Friday. November 18th when we will reveal the free link to the original New York Times article, some questions about the graph, and a few Stat Nuggets.

There will be no graph during the week of Thanksgiving.  But, we will post the graph for the November 30th moderation on Friday, November 18th.  The topic – U.S. life expectancy by group.

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs).
View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 
graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 
Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex). 

Signing off – Sharon Hessney of Boston and David Wilcox of Lawrenceville, New Jersey, one an unpaid college athlete back in the day and the other a professional sports fan.

A trend I noticed in the graph shows younger people along with Black and Latinos agreeing more on the idea that college athletes should be paid based on percentage. The graph also reflects the higher percentage of men who agree with the idea that college athletes should be paid.  

Something which I wonder is why older people tend to believe that college athletes should not be paid, whereas younger people believe otherwise. Part of the curiosity comes from the potential idea that the older generation believed similarly to those of the younger generation at some point, but a change could have changed the belief.

The issue about whether college athletes should be paid relates to my community as it is an issue to where it reflects that despite students being able to get jobs related to the college itself and get paid, student athletes still do not get compensated for their performances. Some college athletes may need the pay in order to help with the family, as the growing need for pay with some athletes becomes an issue with one finding it harder to avoid college, affecting my community and the future generations when it is not guaranteed for pay, unless one gets endorsements.

In the graph, it shows the percentage of people, in a specific group, who either agree, disagree, or are unsure on whether college athletes should be paid. A headline which could be catchy in grabbing the attention of the audience is “Younger population in favor of college athletes getting paid!”

comments.raw_comment:
I noticed that younger people (those under the age of 44 years) make up more than half of the yes percentage on the age graph. Many of those older than 44 voted no making up more than half of the no percentage on this graph. The older the age group, the more people who vote no. Younger people are more affected by this question because they are the ones who are currently in or just graduated college. This may bias their opinion because they are already spending a lot of money to go to college for their studies and are taking in a whole new commitment. Unlike older generations, younger generations have been more focused on college athletics. More men then women also voted yes on this graph. I think this is due to more men playing college sports than women. College women's sports have not always existed and many colleges still don't have select women sports. They may feel men are already having an opportunity they may not have so why should they get paid for it too. 
I wonder how these people in the survey were chosen. Did they all go to college? Did they all play a college sport?
This relates to my community because many of my friends and I are high school athletes looking to make it to the college level. This may upset those who do play a sport at the college level and find out colleges are no longer paying athletes even though they paid those just a few years older than them. 
Headline: Price of a College Athlete

comments.raw_comment:
What do you notice?
From looking at this graph, I notice more black and latino men and women want colleges to pay athletes in comparison to white men and women. Around 69% of both black and latino citizens want colleges to pay their students while only 34% of white citizens are in support of it. 
 
What do you wonder?
From this graph, I wonder why the support for colleges paying their athletes differs when it comes to surveying different ethnicities, genders, and ages. I also wonder how many of those surveyed are college athletes, since I feel that would definitely have an affect on their opinion. 
 
What’s going on in this graph?
In this graph, it represents the public's opinion on whether college athletes should be paid for their participation in college sports. The graph illustrates the responses in three different categories; one bar graph represents the responses between men and women, one represents the responses between black, white, and latino men and women, and the last represents the responses between different ages. 
 
How does this relate to you and your community?
This graph relates to me because I am a senior in high school and this issue is something I personally have an opinion on. It is a topic that I will face in only a couple months and it is helpful to know what the differing opinions are. 
 
Headline: College Athletes: Deserving of Pay?

I noticed that… The youngest respondents to the survey believe that college athletes should be paid and as respondents age increase they are more apprehensive of athletes being paid. I also noticed that almost twice as many minorities, blacks and latinos, believed that college athletes should be paid compared to white respondents. Men also said a higher percentage of college athletes should be paid. 
 
I wonder if… The motivations of money will shift the culture of youth sports and that parents will push their children now to not just get a college scholarship, but to also earn an income. I also wonder whether the divide between female athlete income and male athlete incomes will continue to divide if colleges aren’t equitable in their paychecks.
 
This relates to my community because… I am a student athlete myself, but I take part in running that doesn’t even pay much at the professional level. I know that colleges paying athletes may help some other sports such as football, but track and cross country will most likely not benefit from such an endow. 
 
My name for this graph would be… “At What Cost Do We Support Collegiate Athletes?”

The purple portion of the graph represents those who agree that colleges should pay their athletes. The orange portion represents those who do not believe that colleges should pay their athletes. comments.raw_comment: The graph for today was made from a Marist poll with 1,264 people involved. Age, race, and gender are all factors in whether they agree if colleges should pay athletes. In our findings, we found that typically the younger the person the more they agree with the idea of paying college athletes. Welcome to Wednesday's live moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s graphs display the February 15 – 21, 2022 Marist poll which asked whether college athletes should be paid.  At issue is whether college athletes are employees of their universities.  Some believe that if athletes were paid, this would encourage athletes to cheat and this would affect sports betting.  

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?”, “What do you wonder?"  and “How will this affect you?”  Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas in these graphs. We look forward to replying to your discoveries.

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the online article that included these graphs.  

Note that you can get a link to your response (and replies made to it) to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs).
View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 
graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 
Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex).

What do you notice?
I see that the responses are divided into age, Race/Ethnicity, and Gender, with Yes, No, and Unsure being the options for each. Regarding age, younger respondents were more likely to believe universities should compensate student-athletes, while older respondents were less likely to agree. In terms of race, more Black and Latino voters chose "yes" than "no." Finally, males were more likely than women to believe that colleges should compensate their athletes.

What do you wonder?
I'm curious as to why significantly more Black and Latino people than White people believe that colleges should compensate their student-athletes. I also wonder why the percentages for men and women differ so significantly.

How does this relate to you and your community?
Since many people in the neighborhood are in their final years of high school and will soon be attending college, I can relate this to them. Significant changes may wind up being relevant by the time we are in college because younger generations prefer the idea of colleges paying their student-athletes more and more.

What’s going on in this graph?

1.I saw that 1,264 adults, all of whom were in the US, were included in the poll. Additionally, the older people had been more unsure.Younger individuals feel that athletes should be paid more, whereas older ones say that athletes shouldn't be paid at all.While the majority of white people think colleges shouldn't pay its athletes, the majority of Latino and black people agree that they should.In terms of gender, more men than women support paying athletes.
2.I wonder if the survey pool had any factor in the survey.I wonder if they used an equal amount of people for each section such as the same amount of women and men, the same amount of 18-29-year-olds, and 45-59-year-olds.I wonder why the highest percentage of people who believe colleges should pay their athletes was 18-29-year-olds.I wonder if the graph had more diversity than just white, Latino, and black if it would alter or change the graph significantly. 
3.Because several of my friends are athletes and plan to do so in college, this affects both my community and me.Sports take up a lot of time, therefore I find it puzzling that people are not paid for such a time-consuming activity. comments.raw_comment: A debate that many talks about, Should colleges pay their athletes. Yes, but it depends if they are working hard enough for the sport and doing well in college. After looking at the graph I noticed that the younger the age was: the more said yes. Whereas the older the people were: the more they said no. I wonder why the white race is a much lower percentage than black and Hispanics. Is it because most whites feel like we should work for our money in a real job, not just a college sport? Who knows, but I think it should be much higher, if not, the same as the other races. I also wonder why this graph was just made. I think that it could be because of the payout women get compared to men. I’m not sure if this is always true, but most women think they deserve the same amount as men because they are just as good. But for me, I never watch women's sports because it doesn't entertain me like men's sports would. Which is why I think fewer viewers equals less money.  But in the end, athletes should get paid, even if it's a small amount because every little bit can and will help them greatly with their school, future, and daily life. My catchy headline is, “Pay to play or get paid to play.”

comments.raw_comment:
A perfect example of why I don't always agree with the famous quote "Life's not fair." 
This graph is broken into 3 main stereotypes, then again with an additional 9 stereotypes: separating age, race, and gender. 

          Why is getting paid for a sport, or something many love and endure a career from, a stereotyped issue? I don't understand how it's fair to pay a white person far less than blacks and latinos if they are equal in skill. How is it fair to pay men further more than you're paying a woman? It seems like segregation all over again, and furthermore useless debates for people with way too much time on their hands. Why is this a new issue all of the sudden?

          I'm not big on sports, and in my community I don't hear about this much athletic segregation in my day to day life, fortunately. Yet it is common to hear a guy tell a girl the sport she plays isn't a real sport, because for example, in girls lacrosse tackling and checking sticks past a certain point is illegal, while for boys it's a part of their game of lacrosse. This is an understandable thing to debate about, yet it's unnecessary and not right to do. 

          This graph has the younger black/latino men getting the most gross earnings from the sports they play. To me, this is not fair. I thought we ended slavery years ago, so why reintroduce it to sports?

comments.raw_comment:
I notice that people ages 18 to 29 , the age group of people in college, are the ones who think that they should get paid. And the older groups, especially ages 60 or older, say no. I also notice that the majority of men say they should be paid while the majority women say they shouldn't.
I wonder why these people think that. As a high schooler, I don't see the need to be paid, this is most likely due to the fact that my education is currently free. I also don't play a sport or plan to play a sport, so I don't have the same perspective as the people who do. One thing I would like to see added to this graph is another section of people who do and don't play sports to get another view point. I would assume that the people who play sports would say yes, but I think it would still be interesting to see. 
One idea that I agree with is that they may be compensated for their names, images, or likenesses to be used. I can understand how that would make sense. But to me, it would make sense for them to be paid by the people using those things. Now yes, it may be the colleges, but it may also be: news stations, magazines, newspapers, radio stations, and a few other places. 
The title I came up with is “To or To Not Get Paid? What College Athletes Think.”

comments.raw_comment:
The Fiscal Rate of Athleticism
I hear this question float around the room at nearly all thanksgivings, evoking tight responses from each family member. This is what shocked me about the ten percent margin of 60 and older who were unsure, as my 75 year old grandpa seems to have a pretty good idea about it. That's the difference between theoretical and experimental; we base our theories off of our hypothetical experience(opinions), and experiments off of carrying out the hypothesis to the masses. 
For example, I could have theorized Men have a higher "yes" disposition than the Women (who have a higher "Unsure" disposition than men) due to the fact that I'm aware that society associates athleticism with masculinity. Now, just because I'm aware of this doesn't provide data evidence; I would need some sort of chart to prove my point, with percentages and visuals. Information from a chart I read in a textbook that displayed white people as more economically conservative to draw the conclusion that they would have the highest “No” rate when compared to other races.  This would be a good assignment where social studies students had to predict the demographics based on the question and the percentages, using synthesized information from class to apply to modern day polarizing questions.

comments.raw_comment: In this graph, I notice that up until age 45 the people supported colleges paying for their athletes, but after the answer switched to no. 70% of 18-29-year-olds said yes, 57% of 30-44-year-olds said yes, 36% of 45-59-year-olds said yes, and 29% of 60 or older said yes. I wonder why this is the trend. Why would older people not support colleges paying for their athletes? Why does the answer switch after age 45? This relates to me and my community because I am in High School and going to college in two years. It's important for me to know as a student how people view college payment because when I'm in college, there may be different policies than there are now. People's opinions change policies, if a lot of people don't support the payment, it may not occur in the future. Luckily, the amount of support and non-support is varied and most likely won't cause a major change now. I would name this, "Payment for Performance." The people are saying whether they support the payment for an athlete's performance.

comments.raw_comment:
Evidence shows age, race/ethnicity, and gender impacting opinions
From ages 19-29, the youngest age bracket, 70% of people think that colleges should have paid athletes; most likely because they do not have a career or steady paycheck flowing in yet. So, they would not mind having some extra money earned from their talents to fall back on. In fact, my uncle, who was a college athlete 2 years ago, has talked to me about this topic saying that now, as he is trying to get a job, the extra cash would have been a good jump start to a career. But, as age goes up, so does the number of people who disagree with athletes getting paid; by 60+ only 29% of people voted yes. 

In terms of race/ethnicity, 69% of Black athletes voted yes, 69% of Latinx athletes voted yes, and only 34% of White athletes voted yes. This may be because of financial stature, needing to provide for families, or even just due to the number of athletes at these colleges. Finally, there are more men than women who voted yes. This may be due to the number of male vs female athletes or because of inequality. However, there is not enough evidence in this graph to reflect any of the reasons given above; these are just possibilities. 

In my case, I do think that colleges should pay their athletes because of possible situations at home, extra money to help their future, and because they are helping the college earn money. Without the athletes, there would be no games, no revenue, and no earnings for the college.

comments.raw_comment: The main purpose of this graph is to show what a different variety of people think about college athletes getting paid. I can see why most of the younger people picked "yes" because they're either an athlete in college, an upcoming athlete, or the group that watches college sports the most. The catchy title I decided to go with is Athletes and Accolades.

comments.raw_comment: This is a graph that shows if people think colleges should pay their athletes. When looking at age, it seems that the younger demographic majorly think that athletes should be paid. I suspect this is because college athletes will fall into this category and want to be paid. As the age increases, less and less people argue “yes”. The percentages of unsureness also increases. When looking at race, black people and latinos have the same percentages for “yes”, which is 69%. However, white people have almost half of that percentage. Lastly, for gender, more than half of men think athletes should be paid and about one third of women think the same. I wonder who answered this survey. I also wonder where they and when they did it.
